paragraphs: In the autumn of the nineteenth year of Taiyuan, rain fell on East Mountain for seven days without cease.

Half the paint had peeled from the window lattices of the Xie family’s old house. Each year, as winter approached, the man who tended the fields behind the hill came to replace the roof tiles. He never failed to step inside the hall to look at the Go table. Once, while moving a basin to catch the rain, he accidentally disturbed the boxes of stones. The old servant who watched over the house went so grim-faced that he refused to speak to him even at supper. Afterward they wrapped the wooden boxes in old silk, and whenever heavy rain came again, the servant saved the Go table before ordering anyone to bring the grain in from the yard.

The tiles above the old Xie corridor had cracked. Rain dripped onto the bluestone Go board, barely noticeable by day but making a clear, sharp sound at night. The servant came with a lamp to gather the stones. At the thirty-seventh, his hand stopped. He remembered how Xie An, when he played, would hold a white stone between his fingers until he had finished discussing affairs of state, only then setting it down. In those days the corridor had been filled with distinguished guests, the tea brazier had never cooled, and carriages and horses were forever coming up the mountain road.
Now there was only rain among the pines beyond the corridor.
The servant set the boxes of black and white stones neatly in place again. Then he heard a child shout at the doorway, “These are the Qin soldiers!”

Two children who had come with their parents to shelter from the rain had taken seats at the board while he was inside. The older boy cupped a handful of black stones and heaped them along the northern edge. The younger took only a few white ones and arranged them anxiously in a corner of Jiangnan.
“You can have only those,” said the older. “I have a million soldiers on this side.”
“Lord Xie will help me!” cried the younger.
The older burst out laughing. “Lord Xie is dead!”

The servant meant to scold them, but on reaching the corridor he stopped, not knowing why. The mountains and rivers remained. So did the board. The smaller child was stubbornly pushing a white stone into the thick black encirclement. A drop of water struck it and slid it one line across. Both children collapsed in laughter. The servant crouched to wipe the board dry and sent them somewhere warm so they would not catch cold.

Before long, an envoy arrived from Jiankang. Fine rain had dampened the corners of his sealed letter. He carried greetings from a collateral branch of the Xie family, along with a question now repeated throughout the city: if Grand Tutor Xie were still alive, how would he play this position?
The servant, who could read only a little, studied those words for a long time.
“Tell your young master,” he said, folding the letter, “there is an old Go set here in the mountains. Whoever wishes to play may always come through the gate.”
“And who, in your view, could play it now?” the envoy asked.
The servant did not answer. Beyond the corridor the two children were squabbling over the last white stone. They had already forgotten how the Qin army had retreated.
In the palace of the Imperial City at Jiankang, another game lay spread out.

Sima Daozi had a map of the commanderies of Jiangdong opened before him. A black jade weight held Jingkou, a blue-green one Jingzhou, and a white jade dragon stood over the palace city of Jiankang, its polished surface exceptionally soft in the light. Each time Daozi finished hearing a memorial, he pushed the corresponding weight half an inch across the map. The jade pieces traveled easily. Outside the curtains, the army clerks awaiting answers had already been relieved twice.

“Liu Laozhi is asking for grain again,” said the chief clerk. “The Jingkou camp is behind on pay. Two ration allotments cut the month before last have not been restored. Some soldiers' families are already lighting fires outside the granary to boil grass roots.”
“Restore one month’s allotment first,” said Sima Daozi.
“And the other month?”
“Have the Three Wu districts send supplies. The wealthy families down south tell us the harvest is excellent. It is time they showed the government something for it.”

The chief clerk made a note, then reported on Jingzhou. Yin Zhongkan requested a reduction in the grain tribute and further shipbuilding, claiming conditions along the river had changed. At the words “river conditions,” Sima Daozi laughed. “Let the Yangtze rise a foot and Jingzhou headquarters demands another battalion. Who taught him that?”

The officials lowered their heads. Everyone knew that Jingzhou possessed its own commanders and retainers, Jingkou its soldiers, and the Imperial City its edicts. Without moving from their places, these centers of power had developed enmities as deep as the river.

Suddenly someone outside beat the grievance drum. Palace guards stopped the petitioners in the rain. Voices floated up the stone steps: tenant farmers from Kuaiji and Wu Commandery were accusing great households of seizing their fields, increasing corvée, and charging miscellaneous fees as tax boats passed through their villages. A white-haired woman knelt in a puddle clutching a tattered petition and refused to leave.
“Have the Department of State Affairs accept their petitions,” Sima Daozi said.
“The department says the case belongs to the home commanderies.”
“Then send them home.”
“They fled those very commanderies.”

Daozi raised his eyes. The palace guards understood. They went out with their men. The cries of the petitioners faded together with the clatter of armor, and the discussion inside returned to Jingkou’s grain supply. The white jade dragon stayed motionless at the center of Jiankang.

A few days later, the same reports reached Chang’an. The Qin court’s western hall was reviewing salt prices in Hexi when a bundle of documents brought new affairs of Jiangnan: the Xie family’s influence fading, the Beifu Army short of pay, the Jingzhou garrisons growing stronger, and the imperial clan and commanders of the Imperial City increasingly suspicious of one another. A young officer finished reading and chuckled. “If we had crossed the Fei River in one stroke back then, would we have all this trouble today?”
Fu Jian was taking his medicine. He set the cup down.
“When Xie An stood in Jiangnan with the Fei River between us, I hated him for barring my way. Now he is dead, and Xie Xuan is dead too. Does that truly make Jiangnan easier to conquer?”
“There is no one left in the Xie family to command the Beifu Army,” the officer replied.
“Then the men of Jingkou have forgotten how to wield swords?”

The officer fell silent. Fu Jian ordered the old archives brought out. The correspondence exchanged between the two states during the standoff at the Fei River had been carefully preserved. The paper had yellowed, with rain stains from that year in several places. Unfolding Xie An’s reply, Fu Jian pointed to a rather uneven seal impression in one corner and asked Fu Hong if he recalled who had secured the Jin flotilla on the eastern bank.
“Xie Xuan,” Fu Hong answered.
“And Xie An?”
“In Jiankang, holding off the court officials who kept demanding orders from the men at the front.”

Fu Jian nodded. He instructed the court historians to arrange the relevant documents for the biographies of figures from the enemy state, omitting none of their former opposition to Qin. The young officer looked unconvinced and was about to protest, but his eyes fell on the emperor’s gaunt hand. At last he lowered his head.

Zhu Xu sat in the western guest seats, still dressed in the Jin fashion. He had lived in Chang’an for many years without accepting a ranked Qin office. Occasionally he was asked about the people of old Xiangyang or merchants traveling along the Huai, but he never drew plans of Jin defenses. At the sound of Xie An’s name, he suddenly saw the river fog of years before and the flames above Xiangyang’s walls.
When court ended, he remained behind. After only a few men were left in the hall, he bowed deeply to Fu Jian.
“I wish to go to East Mountain and pay my respects at Grand Tutor Xie’s shrine.”

Fu Hong looked first at his father. Since Zhu Xu had come north, he had never been permitted to cross the frontier without an escort. Many Qin ministers respected him, but the people of Jin might not welcome him. There were guards, interrogations and suspicions on both sides.
“After you have made your offering, what then?” Fu Jian asked.
“I have not yet decided.”
“What if their court forbids you to return?”
“Then I shall die in Jiangnan.”
Fu Jian studied him. “Has life in Chang’an been so disagreeable?”
“I have been able to live here,” Zhu Xu answered. “But I still remember the road home.”

Fu Jian did not try to detain him. He took a sheet from beside his desk, wrote two lines, folded it into an envelope, and left it without an official seal. Zhu Xu was to deliver it to Xie’s family, or, if no suitable recipient could be found, leave it in Xie An’s old house.
“What has Your Majesty written?”
“Open it when you reach East Mountain.”
Zhu Xu took the letter. It weighed almost nothing in his sleeve, yet seemed to add a stone to what he carried.

Traveling east from Chang’an, Zhu Xu saw soldiers of three peoples drawing grain at Guanzhong post stations with the same ration document. He also saw newly repaired embankments north of the Wei cut open at night, leaving county clerks and laborers quarreling in the mud until dawn. East of Luoyang, a Qin relief column marched across a bridge: a Xianbei officer urging his horse forward, a Han cart soldier pulling on a rope. The two were red-faced over who should cross the planks first. When their squad leader arrived, his first order was that they work together to lift a wheel out of the mud. Zhu Xu watched from the roadside a moment, then rode on.
The farther east he went, the more people he met coming north from the south.

At a ferry market, a family of seven huddled outside a temporary porridge shelter. A man held a feverish child; a woman asked whether they could return south after taking a wooden token for temporary residence. An old man kept asking whether they would still be allowed to honor their ancestors. The youngest girl was so tired she slept against a sack of rice. The clerk had talked himself hoarse and complained that they asked the same questions three times, but finally told the physician to take the child first. A local man at the back of the line cursed them for holding up the grain. When he saw that the child’s lips had turned purple, he stepped aside.
Zhu Xu asked the officer at the checkpoint, “Are all these people citizens of Qin now?”
“Who can say? They are here temporarily and we have counted the households. We cannot let them starve in the meantime.”
“And if the Jin court demands their return?”
“The authorities are still discussing it.”

That night Zhu Xu lodged at a checkpoint inn north of the Huai and heard someone outside ordering a boat away from the bank. In the moonlight, the bow rode almost level with the water. Qin soldiers found two short blades and an old bow and immediately separated several of the men. One, whose shoulder bore the old chafing marks of armor, knelt and admitted, “A deserter from the Beifu Army.”

An old woman rushed forward and clung to him. “One of his children is dead already. The army has owed him two months' pay, and now they want to send him to fight in Jingzhou. Officer, arrest him if you must, but do not send the rest of us back.”
The commander ordered the deserter held separately. Zhu Xu stood nearby. Seeing the Jin clothing he wore, the man suddenly asked, “General, will you speak for Jin?”
“I am still a man of Jin.”
“Then tell them I did not bring soldiers over to surrender to Qin. I came to beg food for my mother.”

Zhu Xu gave no promise; he did not know what military case might still lie against the man. But he asked his name and entered it in the small notebook he carried. He watched the officer escort the old woman and children into an inn with a charcoal fire. Only when the wooden door closed did the man turn back and let the Qin soldiers bind his hands.

They crossed the river the next day, with searching inspections on both banks. The Qin soldiers brought them halfway across and turned back; the Jin troops then kept Zhu Xu’s boat on the water for a full hour. A young Jin commandant read his travel papers, saw that he had lived for years in Qin territory, and sneered. “Governor Zhu, whose rivers are you managing now?”
“Those of the people whose fields are being flooded.”
The commandant demanded to open Fu Jian’s private letter. Zhu Xu held it beneath his palm. “It contains no military order. It is addressed to the Xie family.”
“How am I to know that?”
“If you open it without leave, you will not take it away from me.”

They argued until the sun was sinking. At last an elderly lieutenant who recognized Zhu Xu arrived and ordered the boat released. On the southern bank, Zhu Xu saw two peasant women driven away by guards as they tried to cross in search of their sons. A medicine merchant lacking a tax certificate had his whole basket of herbs seized. The rice fields of Jiangnan were green, the distant mountains looked much as they always had, but iron barriers and military tents now stood beside the bridge.

Following the familiar road, he reached East Mountain. Half the timber at the mountain gate had rotted, and rainwater streamed down the bluestone steps. The old house servant looked at him for a long time before calling him “General Zhu.” No one in the courtyard discoursed on metaphysics. The grape arbor was gone. Only the pines and the old Go board remained.

Zhu Xu knelt before Xie An’s spirit tablet and set down a cup of clear wine. Only when the third coil of incense smoke had risen did he take out Fu Jian’s letter. It was short. After the Qin army withdrew north of the Fei, it said, Xie An had both guarded Jin territory and stayed the northern ruler’s rashness for a time. Now Lord Xie was gone, Qin took no joy in Jiangnan’s internal strife, and hoped that the people of both banks might suffer less from war. There was no formal tribute or declaration of submission, only the name “Fu Jian.”
After listening to him read it, the servant asked, “Is this a request that we surrender?”
“No.”
“Does he ask us to trust him?”
“Not that either.”
“Then what would Lord Xie say if he were still here?”
Zhu Xu looked at the lamp before the spirit tablet. “Lord Xie would answer for himself.”

That night a young man of the Xie family came up the mountain through the rain. Seeing the letter, he sneered. “The Heavenly King of the North writes as prettily as anyone. If Jiankang truly falls into disorder, do you think he will refrain from marching?”
“He may well march,” Zhu Xu said.
“Then why carry his letter?”
“I came to honor Lord Xie. I also wanted to see with my own eyes what Jiangnan has become.”

The young man pushed a boardful of white stones toward him. “While the Qin armies stayed north of the river, everyone said Lord Xie had secured the lands south of the Yangtze. But if the northern army comes again today, who will defend them?”

Zhu Xu picked up a stone and held it for a long time without playing. The Beifu Army lacked grain; the Jingzhou forces guarded their own strength; in the palace at Jiankang, officials were still fighting endlessly over a tax order. The boats kept crossing in the night. He would offer no easy words on either side’s behalf.
“Lord Xie did not leave us a game that must be won,” Zhu Xu said, returning the stone to its box. “He left Jiangnan many years. Those years are nearly spent.”

The young man said nothing. He opened the door and walked into the rain. Later that night, a wind stirred the box beneath the eaves, making one or two light taps. Zhu Xu woke and thought someone was placing stones. When he stepped into the corridor, the board was empty. At dawn the old servant counted the white stones and found one missing. After searching for a long time, he discovered it in a shallow gutter beside the steps.
Rain had washed the little white stone clean. The old servant returned it to the lacquered box and closed the lid. Birds called beyond the mountain. Day had broken.
